subject: Manufacturing
summary: orthogonal and oblique cutting, tool signature (ASA and ORS), chip formation and the built-up edge, shear angle, shear strain and velocity relations, Merchant's circle and force analysis, tool wear and tool materials, Taylor's tool life equation, machinability, cutting power and the economics of machining

questions.text: In oblique cutting with a tool of inclination angle i, Stabler's flow rule states that the chip flow angle η (measured on the rake face from the normal to the cutting edge) is
opts: equal to the rake angle
zero, whatever the inclination
approximately equal to the inclination angle i
equal to 90° − i
questions.ans: (C) approximately equal to the inclination angle i
solution: Concept: In oblique cutting the cutting edge is inclined at angle i to the normal of the cutting velocity, so the chip does not flow straight up the rake face.
Stabler found experimentally that the chip flows sideways at an angle η ≈ i, measured on the rake face from the normal to the edge: (C).
In orthogonal cutting i = 0, so η = 0 and the chip flows normal to the edge.
Exam tip: Oblique cutting has three force components (cutting, feed and radial); orthogonal cutting has only two.

questions.text: In orthogonal cutting with a tool of rake angle 15°, the uncut chip thickness is 0.20 mm and the chip thickness is 0.45 mm, as shown. The shear angle (in degrees, round off to two decimal places) is ______
solution: Concept: Volume constancy along the shear plane gives t = l sin φ and tc = l cos(φ − α), so tan φ = r cos α/(1 − r sin α), with r = t/tc.
Exam tip: r is always less than 1 (the chip is thicker than the uncut layer), and a larger r means a larger shear angle and lower forces.

questions.text: In orthogonal cutting with a rake angle of 10°, the shear angle is 30°. The shear strain in the chip is about
solution: Concept: Shear strain in orthogonal cutting: γ = cot φ + tan(φ − α) = cos α/[sin φ cos(φ − α)].
Exam tip: For a given α, γ is minimum when φ = 45° + α/2, the same condition as Merchant's minimum-energy solution with zero friction.

questions.text: A single-point tool is specified in the ASA system as 10-12-8-6-15-20-0.8. The end cutting edge angle of the tool is
solution: Concept: ASA tool signature order: back rake αb, side rake αs, end relief, side relief, end cutting edge angle Ce, side cutting edge angle Cs, nose radius.
So 10° back rake, 12° side rake, 8° end relief, 6° side relief, 15° end cutting edge angle, 20° side cutting edge angle and 0.8 mm nose radius: (D).
Exam tip: In ORS, the principal cutting edge angle φ = 90° − Cs = 70° here, and the auxiliary cutting edge angle φ1 = Ce = 15°.

questions.text: In orthogonal cutting with a tool of rake angle 8°, the cutting force is 1500 N, the thrust force is 600 N and the chip thickness ratio is 0.32. The shear force along the shear plane (in N, round off to one decimal place) is ______
solution: Concept: All the forces are components of the same resultant R, so in the Merchant's circle (see figure) Fs = Fc cos φ − Ft sin φ.
Also F<sub>n</sub> = 1500 sin φ + 600 cos φ = 1041.7 N, F = 802.9 N, N = 1401.9 N and μ = F/N = 0.573.
Exam tip: Fs and Fn come from rotating (Fc, Ft) by φ; F and N come from rotating by α.

questions.text: According to Merchant's theory, if the friction at the tool–chip interface increases while the rake angle remains the same, then
opts: the shear angle decreases, the chip becomes thicker and the cutting force increases
the shear angle increases and the cutting force decreases
the shear angle does not change because it depends only on the rake angle
the chip thickness ratio increases
questions.ans: (A) the shear angle decreases, the chip becomes thicker and the cutting force increases
solution: Concept: Merchant: 2φ + β − α = 90°, so φ = 45° + α/2 − β/2.
A larger friction angle β gives a smaller φ. A smaller φ means a longer shear plane, a smaller chip thickness ratio r (thicker chip) and a larger shear area, so Fc rises: (A).
Exam tip: Cutting fluids, polished rake faces and larger rake angles all raise φ and reduce power.

questions.text: In orthogonal cutting at a cutting speed of 120 m/min with a tool of rake angle 5°, the chip thickness ratio is 0.35. The shear velocity (in m/min, round off to one decimal place) is ______
solution: Concept: The velocity triangle closes: V/cos(φ − α) = Vs/cos α = Vc/sin φ.
Check: chip velocity V<sub>c</sub> = rV = 42 m/min.
Exam tip: Vs can be larger than V; the shear power is FsVs and the friction power is F Vc.

questions.text: For a tool, the Taylor exponent n is 0.2. The tool life is 30 min at a cutting speed of 100 m/min. The cutting speed (in m/min, round off to two decimal places) that gives a tool life of 60 min is ______
solution: Concept: Taylor's equation V Tn = C.
V2 = 87.06 m/min
Exam tip: Because n is small, doubling the tool life needs only about a 13 % cut in speed.

questions.text: For finish turning of a hardened alloy steel (about 60 HRC), the most suitable cutting tool material is
opts: high-speed steel
cubic boron nitride (CBN)
uncoated cemented carbide of the K (cast iron) grade
polycrystalline diamond (PCD)
solution: Concept: The tool must keep its hardness at high temperature and must not react chemically with the work.
CBN is the second hardest material, is stable up to about 1400 °C and is chemically inert to iron, so it is used for hard turning of steels: (B).
Diamond is harder but dissolves in iron (carbon diffusion) at high temperature, so PCD is used for non-ferrous metals and composites. HSS and uncoated carbides soften or wear fast on 60 HRC steel.
Exam tip: Order of hot hardness: HSS < carbides < ceramics < CBN < diamond.

questions.text: The Taylor equation for a tool is VT<sup>0.25</sup> = 250 (V in m/min, T in min). The machine and labour cost is ₹4 per minute, the tool cost per cutting edge is ₹40 and the tool changing time is 1 min. The cutting speed for minimum cost per piece (in m/min, round off to one decimal place) is ______
solution: Concept: For minimum cost, Topt = (1/n − 1)(tc + Ct/Cm).
Exam tip: The speed for maximum production rate (T = (1/n − 1)tc = 3 min) is always higher than the speed for minimum cost.

questions.text: The machinability index (rating) of a material is usually defined as
opts: the hardness of the material relative to that of a free-cutting steel
the ratio of cutting force on the material to that on a free-cutting steel
the surface roughness obtained relative to a free-cutting steel
the cutting speed for a fixed tool life (often 60 min) on the material, as a percentage of that for a standard free-cutting steel
questions.ans: (D) the cutting speed for a fixed tool life (often 60 min) on the material, as a percentage of that for a standard free-cutting steel
solution: Concept: Machinability is judged by tool life, forces/power and surface finish, but the common single-number rating uses tool life.
Machinability index = V60(material)/V60(standard) × 100 %, where the standard is AISI 1112 free-cutting steel (rated 100 %): (D).
Exam tip: A material with index above 100 % (e.g. free-cutting brass, aluminium alloys) is easier to machine than the standard.

questions.text: A bar of 60 mm diameter is turned at 500 rpm with a feed of 0.2 mm/rev and a depth of cut of 1.5 mm. If the specific cutting energy of the work material is 3 J/mm³, the cutting power (in kW, round off to two decimal places) is ______
solution: Concept: Cutting power = specific cutting energy × material removal rate (MRR = V f d).
Exam tip: Specific energy (J/mm³) is numerically the same as the mean pressure Fc/(f d) in N/mm².

questions.text: In machining a ductile metal at moderate to high cutting speed, most of the heat generated is
opts: conducted into the workpiece
carried away by the chip (typically about 70–80 %)
conducted into the tool
radiated to the surroundings
questions.ans: (B) carried away by the chip (typically about 70–80 %)
solution: Concept: Heat is generated in the primary (shear) zone, the secondary (tool–chip) zone and the tertiary (flank–work) zone.
At usual cutting speeds the chip moves away fast and carries most of the heat: (B); roughly 10–20 % goes into the work and about 5–10 % into the tool.
Exam tip: The share taken by the chip increases with cutting speed, which is why high-speed machining can keep the work cool.

questions.text: A tool obeys the extended Taylor equation VT<sup>0.25</sup>f<sup>0.6</sup> = C. If the feed is halved, the percentage increase in cutting speed that keeps the same tool life (round off to one decimal place) is ______
solution: Concept: For constant T, V f0.6 = constant, so V2/V1 = (f1/f2)0.6.
V<sub>2</sub>/V<sub>1</sub> = 2<sup>0.6</sup> = 1.5157
Increase = 51.6 %
Exam tip: Tool life is most sensitive to speed, less to feed and least to depth of cut, so to raise MRR without losing tool life, increase depth first, then feed.

questions.text: In orthogonal cutting, if the rake angle of the tool is increased while the other conditions remain the same,
opts: both the chip thickness ratio and the shear angle increase, and the cutting force decreases
both the chip thickness ratio and the shear angle decrease
the shear angle increases but the chip thickness ratio decreases
the chip thickness ratio increases but the cutting force also increases
questions.ans: (A) both the chip thickness ratio and the shear angle increase, and the cutting force decreases
solution: Concept: From Merchant, φ = 45° + α/2 − β/2, and r = sin φ/cos(φ − α).
A larger α gives a larger φ; a larger φ gives a shorter shear plane and a thinner chip, i.e. a larger r. The smaller shear area lowers Fc: (A).
Exam tip: The limit to raising the rake angle is the strength of the tool wedge, which is why carbides and ceramics often use negative rake.
